context_after.text: For this investigation, a test solution of deaerated (nitrogen purge) 1 N sulfuric acid containing 0.5 M NaCl was chosen. The test temperature was 27 C.Other parameters common to most tests included a 9-μm diamond paste surface finish and a 3-V/h potential scan rate.

The schematic polarization curve shown in Figure 1 is typical when pitting occurs; shown along the curve are some of the important values characterizing the response of the alloy to the test. The test begins at the open circuit potential (Ec). Once a stable active $\tt E _ { c }$ value was achieved, the sample was polarized anodically at (typically) 3 V/h. The polarization continues through the critical passivation current density (CD) $(\mathfrak { i } _ { \circ }),$ through the passive potential range up to the pitting potential $(\ E _ { \mathsf { p i t } })$, at which the CD dramatically increases. Polarization is continued to $E _ { m a x },$ the potential at which pitting has propagated sufficiently to increase the sample CD to $1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ A/cm². The scan direction is then reversed and stopped at the potential where the reverse scan CD equals the upscan CD $(E _ { \mathfrak { r } }$ —repassivation potential). The magnitude of the CD at which the polarization scan was reversed was chosen to represent a compromise between a value large enough to ensure the onset of stable pitting and one small enough to enable microstructural determination of the majority of pit initiation sites.

context_after.text: Using this concept, pitting potential data for solution-treated (1 h, 1120 C, water quench) CF alloys are presented in Figure 3. The normalizing function describing ${ \mathsf { C r } } _ { \mathsf { e f f } }$ is the sum of the weight percentage of Cr and Mo in the austenite plus 20 times that of the carbon and nitrogen in the austenite. Restricting the $\mathsf { C r } _ { \mathsf { e f f } }$ calculation to the composition of the austenite phase is based on the observation that, in every case, pits form exclusively in the austenite phase or at the ferrite-austenite boundaries. In no instance were pits located in the ferrite phase. It should be pointed out that the composition of the austenite phase was not measured analytically but was approximated using partitioning data for Cr between ferrite and austenite in similar alloys⁸ and assuming that all of the nitrogen and carbon in the alloy is in the austenite. Neither approach is exact, but, to a first approximation, they are more appropriate than calculation of $\mathsf { C r } _ { \mathsf { e } \# }$ based upon the bulk composition. The specific form of this ${ \mathsf { C r } } _ { \mathsf { e f f } }$ (including the role of carbon) evolved as a portion of this research² and will not be developed here. For the alloys under consideration (Table 1, Figure 3), nitrogen is the major compositional variable because the Cr and Mo are essentially constant and only CF-3 has a carbon content outside the range of 0.05 to 0.06% carbon.

The pitting potentials plotted in Figure 3 were determined using samples prepared as previously described; specific to these data were a test temperature of 27 C, a potential scan rate of 3 V/h, and a 9-μm surface finish (including the aforementioned masking procedure) just prior to immersion in the solution of 1 N sulfuric acid and 0.5 M NaCl. (These conditions will be referred to as the standard test conditions.) The data points, all for solutiontreated CF alloys, represent the average of at least three determinations, with the vertical bars representing the total scatter in the values. A trend identical to that in Figure 3 was found for a wide range of conditions, such as 9-μm to 1 grit surface finish, 27 to 42 C solution temperature, and 0.05 to 3.0 V/h scan rate, but this discussion will emphasize the specific results shown Figure 3.

The solid portion of Figure 9 is an expanded potential scale plot of the anodic loop for the highest nitrogen $(\mathsf { C r } _ { \mathsf { e n } })$ alloy. That the active dissolution polarization curve comprises two components is also suggested by the data in Figure 10. This graph compares the relative positions of the active corrosion peaks of CF-11 (low nitrogen) and CF-4 (high nitrogen) with the active corrosion curves of pure iron and pure chromium. It is apparent that the curve for CF-4 is very similar to pure iron during the initial stages of active dissolution. This suggests that nitrogen encourages the active dissolution of iron—and/or retards the dissolution of chromium—and thus enriches the remaining metal surface in chromium. It is, therefore, proposed that the anodic loop for high nitrogen alloys is composed of a low potentia/ loop that represents iron being preferentially dissolved (thus leaving chromium behind) in a magnitude proportional to the nitrogen content and a high potential loop that is representative of all CF alloys

Although a possible explanation for this phenomenon is that the two “separate" peaks represent dissolution of the austenite and ferrite phases, arguments may be made rejecting this possibility. First, the separation or splitting into two peaks is observed only for alloys of total nitrogen in austenite near or above 0.12% N. Equally important is the fact that the anodic loop splitting is observed in wholly austenitic alloys with nitrogen contents near or above 0.12% N, as shown in this research² and elsewhere.9 Anodic loop splitting has also been observed in duplex alloys containing nitrogen, but the authors8.14 suggested that the behavior was controlled by the degree of chromium segregation between the ferrite and austenite or that it represented differentiation in the onset of passivation for the two phases. Obviously, neither of these completely explains this phenomenon because of similar results for wholly austenitic alloys.

context_before.text: Several variations in procedure were used to test the hypothesis that the low potential loop is related to the alloy nitrogen content and that the dissolution that occurs at this potential influences the pitting resistance. The first variation was to perform pitting experiments on the high-nitrogen alloys in which the potential was changed in such a manner that allowed the lower potential loop to be omitted, or at least have its influence minimized. This was done by performing exactly the same cyclic polarization procedure as the previously described test, with the exception that the potential region from a few millivolts below $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { c } }$ up to a potential of -80 mV (corresponding to a potential near, but just below, the peak of the high potential loop of Figure 9) was scanned very quickly (>200 V/h). At this point, the potential scan was allowed to proceed normally. This procedure of omitting the potential range from near $\ E _ { \mathrm { { c } } }$ to -80 mV was performed on the CF-11 (low nitrogen) alloy as well. The results, shown in Figure 12, indicate that this procedure has no effect on the CF-11 alloy (because no “important” portion of the anodic loop was omitted) but that the CF-3 and -4 alloys show a significant drop in the value of $\Xi _ { \mathsf { p i t } }$ when the lower loop is omitted in the upscan. Thus, some factor relating to the higher corrosion resistance of the high-nitrogen alloys is influential in the potential region that was omitted.

The polarization curve in Figure 13 is representative of this evaluation procedure. It indicates that while the net current was still cathodic, the potential was rapidly moved from just below $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { c } }$ to -80 mV in ~2 s. In the high-nitrogen alloys (CF-3 and -4), upon reaching –80 mV, a large anodic current surge of 2 to 3 s occurred. In the low-nitrogen alloy (CF-11), this current surge did not occur. In addition to having an $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { p i t } }$ considerably below the $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { p } \mathsf { i } \mathsf { t } }$ predicted by the standard procedure, the high-nitrogen alloys also exhibited uncharacteristic large current excursions at potentials below $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { p i t } }$ that are absent during the standard procedure. Also significant is the fact that, by virtue of omitting the low potential loop for the high-nitrogen alloys, the pit initiation sites changed from predominantly ferrite-austenite boundary locations to exclusively within the austenite phase. As shown earlier, the austenite more readily pits (as measured by $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { p i t } })$ unless the austenite is somehow made more pit resistant such that the ferrite-austenite interface is more susceptible to pitting as the potential is increased. Thus, mechanisms exist to enhance the pitting resistance of the passive film on the austenite if the potential scan includes the low potential loop. It appears that the current surge that occurs for the highnitrogen alloys at -80 mV is sensitive to the nitrogen content and hence to the beneficial retention of chromium in the passive film. If this were not the case, the pitting potential of the high-nitrogen alloys would be identical to that for the low-nitrogen CF-11 alloy for which this current surge does not occur. Its absence for the CF-11 alloy also implies that dissolution is encouraged by nitrogen during the current surge for the high-nitrogen alloys. The influence of scanning through the potential range of the lower loop is further demonstrated by the folowing sequence. Following omission of the anodic loop below -80 mV for the high-nitrogen alloys, the potential was scanned back down into the low potential loop region prior to completion of the pitting test. On subsequent scanning to the pitting potential range, $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { p i t } }$ values essentially equal to those resulting from a continuous scan from $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathsf { c } }$ are observed for the high-nitrogen alloys.

context_after.text: As intended, the maximum anodic currents for the samples polarized in chloride-free sulfuric acid are all about at factor of 30 lower than for the equivalent alloy in the standard solution (~4.5 x $1 0 ^ { - 5 } \times 5 1. 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } A / (c m ^ { 2 }$, respectively). Despite the lower anodic currents, the Figure 15 data nevertheless indicate some benefit of solid solution nitrogen in terms of pitting resistance. This suggests that whenever nitrogen is present in the alloy, independent of the actual size of the anodic loop, chromium tends to be retained in the passive film. Figure 16 indicates that the open circuit potential of the alloys in the chloride-free sulfuric acid varies as a function of nitrogen in a very similar fashion to the $\mathsf { E } _ { \mathrm { c } }$ values for the standard test solution, although the values in the presence of chloride are ~140 mV lower. Chlorides are known to increase the anodic CD in the active potential range more than the CD for the cathodic reaction; hence, the decrease in E in the presence of chlorides is to be expected. The general conclusion, however, is that nitrogen may exert an influence on the active dissolution behavior for a wide range of environments.

In view of the preceding discussion, it seems plausible to suggest that the role of nitrogen is related to chromium enrichment at/near the surface in these alloys. On an atomic scale, it is not known by what mechanism this occurs. It can be speculated that, because of the known affinity of chromium for nitrogen, the fact that nitrogen slows chromium diffusion in the austenite16,17 and that nitrogen accumulates at the metal/oxide interface during corrosion,18 chromium is retained in the passive film (and near surface layers) because of a chromium/nitrogen interaction (similar to a clustering effect), which inhibits both diffusion and dissolution. This specific mechanism, however, has not been verified.

The present research, through critical manipulation, observation, and analysis of cyclic polarization curves as a function of nitrogen content of the CF alloys, has led to a description of a mechanism of the improvement in pitting resistance resulting from nitrogen additions. It is hypothesized that the change in shape and position of the anodic loop as a function of nitrogen content results from contributions from two dissolution processes that occur in a magnitude related to the amount of nitrogen in austenite. Specifically, for high-nitrogen contents, the anodic loop of the cyclic polarization curve splits into two active loops. The high potential loop was found to be common to all alloys of this general composition class, but the low potential loop increased in magnitude and occurred at lower potentials as the nitrogen content increased. The observation that this low potential loop closely resembles the polarization curve for the active dissolution of iron in similar solutions suggests that nitrogen encourages the dissolution of iron and the accumulation of chromium during the initial stages of active dissolution.

context_after.text: The pitting of high-nitrogen alloys was observed to be very sensitive to procedure variations designed to vary the influence of the active dissolution processes occurring on passing through the low potential loop (i.e., during the early stages of active dissolution). The pitting test results for the low-nitrogen alloys were not influenced by these procedure variations.

It was also shown, with atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS), that increasing nitrogen in CF alloys decreases the amount of chromium found in solution following potentiostatic dissolution at a variety of potentials. Since the chromium content of the solution is lower with increasing nitrogen content of the alloy, chromium must be accumulating at the surface (in the passive film or near surface layers) of the nitrogen-containing alloys. Thus, in the presence of solid solution nitrogen, the surface chromium content of the alloy is effectively increased and the pitting resistance is observed to improve. The observed trend of the nitrogen effect on chromium accumulation was observed at al dissolution potentials examined, but this effect was greatest for active dissolution at potentials near that of the low potential loop.

context_after.text: It is suggested that the completion of an anodic loop potential scan is not necessary to develop pitting resistance resulting from nitrogen additions. During the initial burst of current associated with a pit embryo, active dissolution conditions exist. In the presence of nitrogen, this current burst contains predominantly iron ions and the pit surface remaining becomes relatively enriched in chromium and thus may repassivate more easily than in the absence of nitrogen. This was observed experimentally in the cyclic polarization curves for CF alloys. In the passive potential region (below the pitting potential), the high-nitrogen alloys exhibit much smaller (and fewer) current excursions than the low-nitrogen alloys prior to the onset of stable pitting. In addition, the high-nitrogen alloys were observed to exhibit some tendency toward partial repassivation at potentials above that determined to be the pitting potential.

Finally, it is proposed that, on an atomic scale, the affinity of nitrogen for chromium discourages chromium dissolution resulting from a clustering type of effect. Although the clustering-type mechanism was not analytically proven, this concept is consistent with other observations noted in the literature, such as the facts that nitrogen retards chromium diffusion in the austenite and that nitrogen accumulates at the metal/oxide interface of SSs during corrosion.
